measured_by: The exchange; one state against the rest of the country in the same winter
family: two short gains that rhyme, one for the body, one for the dream
why: Two gains in five words, so short that it fits on a train [mine]. One state was flooded instead of the country being sprinkled, so everybody there saw it many times [mine].
for_client: A dairy in one city only: every tram and bakery bag carries 'Milk for the bones — meadow for the eyes.' Film: the milk train's side slides past a grey street with those words, a child turns; then the bottle.
source: American Heritage, 'A Social History of the Singular Fruit'
doubt: Free samples and a lecture train were part of it; the railway wanted settlers too (the second half of the line).
depends_on: Enough money or presence to be everywhere in one place.

opening: Look at All THREE!
picture: Walter Chrysler himself leans over the hood of his cheap Plymouth and speaks to the reader like a salesman in the showroom.
beat: 16% of the low-price market before; the two bigger makers launching new cars the same week
result: sales up 218%; share of the low-price car market from 16% to 24% in one year
measured_by: Trade history; sales and share of the low-price market
family: go and compare me with the two big ones
why: A small maker who tells you to look at the rivals first sounds sure of himself [mine]. It moves him from one of many to one of three in five syllables [mine].
for_client: A young kitchen maker against two chains: the owner leans on his own counter, looks at us: 'Go and see the other two first.' Cut to him handing over a list with both rivals' addresses; then his workshop and date for a visit.
source: Sounds Profitable, 'Ad Wars: comparative advertising' (with links to Riding the Roller Coaster and the Advertising Age encyclopedia)
doubt: A new engine came with it; another source says the 218% was reached within three months.
depends_on: The product must win, or draw, when people do compare.

opening: COMPUTERS FROM IOWA?
picture: A full page of green pasture at evening with grazing cows walking right up to the lens; the beige computers and two big prices are laid over the field.
beat: page after page of grey computer ads with higher prices beside it
result: sales from $1.5 million (1987) to $12 million (1988) and $70.6 million (1989), 2.5% of revenue spent on marketing
measured_by: Company histories; yearly sales
family: the last place you would expect it from
why: The question is what the reader himself is thinking, and the cows answer before the price does [mine]. Nobody else in that magazine could use that picture, because nobody else had the farm [mine].
for_client: A village workshop that makes ski bindings: wide shot of sheep in snow, they part, a bench with bindings stands between them; on screen 'Ski bindings. From sheep people?' then the price and 'made on this farm'.
source: Such Bad Tech Ads, 'Gateway 2000, part 1' (scan of Byte, November 1988, seen); yearly sales also in EBSCO and Encyclopedia.com
doubt: The price was the lowest on the pages around it; several ads ran in the same year. EBSCO links the first cow ad to the 1988 rise.
depends_on: A real, unlikely home, and a price that holds.

opening: PASCAL $49.95 / Hang on to your seats! It’s Turbo Pascal.
picture: Only two things can be read from across the room: the word PASCAL and $49.95 in fat pink neon letters; below, three pairs of bars set it against the rival, a small table gives the rival's price, $595.
seller: Borland International — Turbo Pascal, by mail
beat: rival compilers at several hundred dollars, printed in the ad's own table ($595.00)
result: one full-page ad got the company running: 1,100 orders in the first month, 2,500 in the second
measured_by: The founder, in interviews (Inc. 1989; Micro Cornucopia 1984 as quoted); orders counted
family: a professional tool at a pocket-money price, price as the headline
why: The buyer knows the thing and its usual price, so the number alone is the whole story [mine]. The bars under it answer the next doubt: is it any good? [mine]
for_client: A dental laboratory that prints night guards: poster and 5-second film with only 'NIGHT GUARD' and the price in huge letters; three bars (time, thickness, price) shrink beside the usual ones; a hand drops the guard on the table; 'Send the scan today.'
source: Inc., interview with Philippe Kahn, March 1989 (order counts: Kahn quoted on Hacker News from Micro Cornucopia, December 1984; scan of the ad seen)
doubt: Founder's own account; the order counts come second-hand. The Inc. page sets Byte in italics.
depends_on: Buyers who already know what the thing normally costs.

opening: FINALLY, A CHRONOGRAPH THAT KEEPS UP WITH AMAZING WALT STACK.
picture: A lean old man runs toward us in a runner's shirt, smiling; above him a steel digital watch. Text in three columns tells his mad daily routine before it tells the watch.
seller: The Sharper Image — RealTime running watch, $69, by mail
beat: a similar famous digital watch at $300
result: a $1,000 ad brought $10,000 in sales; later a thousand watches a month for a year
measured_by: The owner, in interviews; sales per ad
family: the hardest user is the proof
why: A 70-year-old who runs 17 miles a day is stranger and surer than any claim about a watch [mine]. The word 'finally' says that other watches failed him [mine].
for_client: A shop for children's shoes: the postwoman who climbs 600 steps a day; film opens on her boots on stairs, voice: 'Finally, a sole that keeps up with Hatice.' She does not stop; the counter runs 1…600; then the shoe and its price.
source: The Hustle, 'How one man built the Sharper Image' (reproduction of the ad seen)
doubt: The owner's own figures; the company failed thirty years later for other reasons. Another account calls the first Runner's World ad a $30 stopwatch that made a small profit.
depends_on: A real, locally known hard user who says yes.

opening: Hear What You’ve Been Missing
picture: The small radio and its sound (the ad's picture is not described by the source).
beat: “New sound system” — a headline about its newness, for the same product
result: 45% lift in sales
measured_by: Told by Robert Cialdini, who worked on it, in a keynote reported live; N not given
family: what you are losing, instead of what is new
why: Something new makes people wait; something they are missing makes them move [source: Cialdini].
for_client: A window maker whose glass keeps out street noise: black screen, only a blackbird sings; text: 'Hear what you have been missing.' Cut to the old window opening and the traffic roar; then the new pane closes and the bird is back. Price per window.
source: Bruce Clay live blog of Robert Cialdini's Pubcon keynote; same case told by Cialdini at PBS NewsHour (without the number)
doubt: Bose has published no figure; the number is Cialdini's; N and dates not given.
depends_on: The old thing must really lack something the buyer can sense at once.

opening: [Columbia Record Club: choose your free records from a list of thirty-two]
beat: the same offer with twelve records to choose from
result: the response rate doubled; 1958 was the best year in the club's history
measured_by: Wunderman's test ad, as told by Malcolm Gladwell from Wunderman's book; response rate; N not given
family: a wider table to choose from
why: People took the same number but came more readily when the table was long [source: Wunderman, from Italian antipasto tables].
for_client: A box-meal kitchen: film of one hand pushing dish after dish into frame until thirty-two small plates fill the table; on screen 'Pick any three. First box.' Then the order page.
source: The New Yorker, Malcolm Gladwell, 'The Spin Myth', 6 July 1998
doubt: Exact words of the ad not printed. More choice has lowered buying in other studies; here the choice was of free things. A music club: show it with goods that fit us.
depends_on: The choice costs the customer nothing and every item is already liked.

opening: [A little gold box in the corner of the ad: find it and take one more record free]
picture: A small gold box printed in the corner of every coupon; a cheap TV spot only tells people to look for the buried treasure.
beat: McCann-Erickson's polished awareness TV spots for the same print ads in other markets: 19.5%
result: responses up by eighty per cent; before it no magazine on the schedule was profitable, after it every one was
measured_by: Wunderman's agency against a rival agency, matched markets; coupons counted
family: a secret hidden in an ordinary coupon
why: The viewer stopped being an audience and became a player who knows something others walk past [source: Wunderman].
for_client: A supermarket leaflet: the shop's 6-second film shows only a finger tapping: 'There is a small blue fish somewhere in Thursday's leaflet. Find it, tell the cashier, take a bread.' No price, no list.
source: The New Yorker, Malcolm Gladwell, 'The Spin Myth', 1998; the 80% / 19.5% contest is told in several case notes
doubt: TV and print worked together; the extra record was the prize.
depends_on: Two media, the one pointing into the other; a prize that costs little.

opening: For the past three or four years things have been going pretty well at our house. We pay our bills, afford such luxuries as having the children’s tonsils out, and still have something in the bank at the end of the year.
picture: A personal letter; it says that only 23 other men receive it.
seller: Bruce Barton for Berea College (education of poor mountain children)
beat: ordinary printed appeals
result: 24 letters, every one of the men gave at least $1,000: 100 per cent response
measured_by: The college's own magazine and SOFII; N = 24
family: a friend talks about his own house before he asks
why: A rich man tells other rich men quietly that he has enough and is restless, which each of them has thought himself [mine]. The letter says how few received it, so nobody can hide in a crowd [mine].
for_client: A craftsman-school founder writes by hand to twenty shop owners of his town: 'Things have gone rather well in our shop these last years. The lease is paid, the boy has his braces…' and asks each for one apprentice's bench, its price and whose name stands on it.
source: SOFII exhibit 'The major donor mailing that achieved 100 per cent response' (letter printed in full); Berea College Magazine 2012
doubt: A famous writer to men who knew him: the list was half of it. Very small N. The letter refers to the church in passing.
depends_on: The writer is one of them and gives first.

opening: As Chairman of the Admiral Richard E. Byrd Polar Center, it is my privilege to invite you to become a member of an expedition which is destined to make both news and history. It will cost you $10,000 and about 26 days of your time. Frankly, you will endure some discomfort, and may even face some danger.
picture: A seven-page personal letter on the chairman's own paper; no brochure.
seller: Admiral Richard E. Byrd Polar Center — flight over both poles (Hank Burnett)
beat: not given
result: all 50 seats at $10,000 filled, from a mailing that cost $5,000
measured_by: Told by two direct-mail archives; seats sold; N = 50 seats
family: honour first, price and danger in the second breath
why: Price, length and danger are told before the reader has settled, so the wrong people leave and the right ones lean in [mine]. He is asked to join, not to buy [mine].
for_client: A wooden-boat school: letter and 10-second film, the builder by the keel, to camera: 'It will cost you €4,000 and nineteen Saturdays. Your hands will hurt. In September your boat goes into the water with your name on it.' Twelve places.
source: Info Marketing Blog, 'Admiral Byrd' (letter in full; the result in a reader's account quoted there); Game of Conversions: 'every spot sold'; opening also in Strategy Online 1999
doubt: No ledger is shown; the count comes from trade retelling; rich, hand-picked lists.
depends_on: A truly rare place with a true limit and a person of standing who signs.

opening: The bug-eyed bird on our envelope who’s ogling you with such distemper has a point. He’s a native American sandhill crane and you may be sitting on top of one of his nesting sites.
picture: On the envelope a sandhill crane with bulging eyes stares at the reader as if displeased (from the letter's own words).
beat: every challenger mailed against it, the writer's own included
result: not beaten for 12 years
measured_by: The writer, in an interview of 1998; the mailing stayed the control for 12 years
family: an animal accuses you, kindly
why: The bird looks at you with a reason, and the first line gives it: you sit on his home [mine]. It jokes about a guilt that others shout about [mine].
for_client: A beekeeper selling honey and bee-hotels: close on a bee's face looking into the lens, held two seconds; voice: 'The lady giving you that look has a point. Your terrace was her meadow.' Then a small wooden hotel is hung; price, one jar free.
source: Chief Marketer, 'The Man Who Invented the Johnson Box' (interviews 1998-1999 with Frank Johnson)
doubt: The writer's own account; no response figure printed.
depends_on: A creature whose claim on the reader is true.

opening: Read 300 Business Magazines in 30 minutes
beat: not given
result: helped to sell 60,000 subscriptions at $36 a year
measured_by: Interview with the writer in The Creators, 1975; subscriptions sold
family: an impossible heap made small
why: Two numbers fight each other: 300 against 30 [mine]. The busy man sees at once what he will no longer have to do [mine].
for_client: A cleaning-supply wholesaler for hotels: film of 300 price lists falling on a desk like a landslide, cut, one sheet laid on the empty desk; on screen '300 price lists. 3 minutes.' Then where to subscribe.
source: Info Marketing Blog, reprint of the Eugene Schwartz interview in The Creators, 1975
doubt: 'Helped': other ads and mailings ran beside it.
depends_on: The heap must be a real chore of the reader's week.

opening: Be the first person on your block to own a Kangaroo
picture: A magazine page that offers a live kangaroo as first prize for naming a new aeroplane; a stuffed koala for the second.
seller: Qantas — flights from the US (Howard Gossage)
beat: the usual lesson about an unknown country
result: one insertion in The New Yorker brought over 7,500 replies
measured_by: Trade history (Marketing.ie, from Harrison's biography of Gossage); replies counted
family: an absurd prize offered with a straight face
why: A prize nobody could house is funnier and more talked of than a ticket [mine]. Naming something makes it a little one's own [mine].
for_client: A furniture shop with a new sofa that has no name: film of a donkey standing calmly in the showroom, on screen 'Name our sofa. Win Karabaş.' Small: 'Second prize: the sofa.' Send the name to…
source: Marketing.ie, 'A towering ad talent'; same count at 42courses.com
doubt: Replies, not tickets. Sources word the headline differently ('first in your block', 'win a Kangaroo').
depends_on: A prize that is really given and a question anyone can answer.

opening: You’ve failed many times, although you may not remember.
seller: United Technologies — company page in The Wall Street Journal
beat: the other messages of the same series: 21,000 to 28,000 letters
result: 123,000 reprint requests and 36,000 letters, the most letters of any in the series; the series 4,225,000 reprints
measured_by: The company's own count, printed by its chief; letters and reprint requests
family: a truth about you, told kindly
why: It begins with a fact about the reader which is both true and forgotten, so he reads on to be forgiven [mine]. Nothing is sold, so he lets it in [mine].
for_client: A driving school for nervous adults: 8-second film, a child's first wobbling steps, seen from behind; text one line at a time: 'You fell down the first time you tried this.' 'You do not remember.' Then a hand takes a car key; number to call.
source: Borden's Blather, 'Gray Matter' (company's figures by Harry Gray); text of the ad on the same site, 2 May 2016
doubt: Letters and reprints, not sales. Opening words read on jborden.com/2016/05/02.
depends_on: Nothing is asked for in return.

opening: [A small card found on the ground: bring it to the Heinz stand and get a free souvenir — a little green pickle]
picture: A printed card scattered over the fairground; at the top of the long stairs a tiny green pickle with a hook, to wear.
seller: H. J. Heinz Company — at the Chicago World's Fair
beat: the same stand on the second floor on the first days: hardly a visitor
result: one million pickle charms given away; police had to control the crowds and beams had to be added to the floor
measured_by: Pennsylvania Heritage; charms given out
family: a lucky find that must be redeemed
why: A card found on the ground feels like luck and not like an advertisement [mine]. The gift can be worn, so every taker becomes a sign for the next [mine].
for_client: A toy shop on the third floor of an arcade: tiny brass keys lie on the ground floor's benches, each with a tag 'This opens something on floor 3.' Film: a child finds one, runs up the stairs, opens a small drawer; the shop's name.
source: Pennsylvania Heritage, 'Heinz: much more than 57 varieties'
doubt: Visitors and charms, not sales, were counted; Wikipedia counts over 100 million pins since.
depends_on: A small thing worth wearing, and a place people would not climb to.

opening: [Four sticks of gum in an envelope, to every address in the telephone book]
picture: An unexpected envelope in the post with four sticks of chewing gum.
seller: Wm. Wrigley Jr. Company — chewing gum
beat: advertising only talks of the taste
result: sent to all 1.5 million listed addresses in 1915 and repeated four years later, to 7 million
measured_by: Company histories; the owner paid for it twice, the second time nearly five times as large
family: the first taste comes to the house
why: What is in the mouth needs no promise [mine]. In 1915 the telephone book was a list of people who could buy, so nothing was wasted [mine].
for_client: A tea house posts two tea bags in a plain envelope to every office on one street: no letter, only 'It is four o'clock.' Film: an office, the envelope opened, steam rises; the house's door, forty metres away.
source: Encyclopedia.com, Wrigley, William, Jr.; 1.5 million addresses: Encyclopedia.com company history and Saturday Evening Post
doubt: No order count; sales were already rising through other advertising.
depends_on: A sample that fits an envelope and a list of real buyers.

opening: [A jigsaw puzzle to cut out: a village street with people carrying sacks of flour; solve it and get a pincushion shaped like a flour sack]
picture: The back page of a national magazine in pieces: when put together, a little village whose people all carry sacks of Gold Medal flour home.
beat: not given
result: 30,000 completed puzzles came in, with several hundred letters of questions that gave birth to Betty Crocker
measured_by: The company's own history; N = 30,000
family: put the picture together yourself
why: Hands that are busy with the picture look at the sack for half an hour [mine]. The prize is tiny and belongs to the kitchen, so it draws cooks and not hunters of prizes [mine].
for_client: A tile maker: the film shows nine tiles in the wrong order; the caption: 'Put the street in order, tell us what the cat is carrying, and the coaster is yours.' Each tile carries a piece of his own workshop.
source: General Mills, 'How Betty Crocker got its start'; picture from Hennepin History Museum
doubt: Replies, not sales; headline words not printed.
depends_on: A picture pleasant enough to finish and a small sure prize.

opening: Hello Boys! Make Lots of Toys!
beat: not given
result: in 30 years he sold 30 million Erector sets
measured_by: Yale Alumni Magazine; sets sold over 30 years under the same slogan in national magazines
family: a grown man calls the child by name of his kind
why: It greets the one who will use it and gives him a verb [mine]. Rhyme makes it a thing boys repeat [mine].
for_client: A shop for children's garden tools: the old gardener looks over a fence straight at us: 'Hello small people! Dig big holes!' He throws a spade; a child catches it; the set and its price.
source: Yale Alumni Magazine, 'Renaissance man'
doubt: Thirty years of many ads, shop windows and the toy itself; the slogan was the constant.
depends_on: The speaker is the maker and means it.

opening: Look inside for your Liberty Rewards
picture: The same plain envelope with the shop's logo, plus this one line on the outside.
beat: the same envelope with the logo only
result: redemption of the vouchers inside rose 'by 5% to 60% overall'; more for high spenders
measured_by: Royal Mail MarketReach with the shop; N not given
family: say what is in the envelope and that it is yours
why: Eyes look at an envelope for a moment; a plain 'yours, inside' tells them not to throw it away [mine].
for_client: A pharmacy's birthday card: envelope with only 'Your free blood-pressure check is in here'. Film: thumb about to bin the post, reads, stops, opens; the date.
source: Royal Mail MarketReach case study on getmemedia.com, 27 April 2012
doubt: The case sheet words the gain two ways: 'by 5% to 60% overall' and 'from 5% to 60%'; the rise is sure, its size is not.
depends_on: Something of worth really is inside.

opening: [Everything the letter had to say, printed on the outside of the envelope]
picture: A bare envelope whose outside is the whole letter: what the bundle is, what it costs, what is in it; nothing is hidden inside.
beat: the seller's previous mailings to the same people who had ignored all of them
result: 44% uplift in customer response against previous averages; 57% lower cost per new customer
measured_by: DMA Awards entry, reported by Royal Mail MarketReach; N not given
family: no envelope secret at all
why: People who expect a trick stop at a seller who says everything before they open [mine]. The bareness is itself the promise of a simple product [mine].
for_client: A phone-repair shop's flyer folded like a letter with all seven prices on the outside and the line 'That was all.' Film: hands turn the paper over, the back is empty, pause; the address.
source: Marketreach case study (DMA Awards, Best Use of Mail)
doubt: Compared with past averages, not with a rival in the same week; the words are not printed.
depends_on: An offer simple enough to stand on an envelope.

opening: [A small packet of cake sprinkles, 'hundreds and thousands', falls out of the letter]
picture: An envelope with a little bag of 'hundreds and thousands' cake decorations and an invitation to hold a tea party.
seller: Breast Cancer Care — Strawberry Tea parties
beat: the control cell without it
result: 4.2% response, outperforming the control cell by 1,400%; cold people 97% better than supporters; return projected at 9.2:1
measured_by: Royal Mail MarketReach with the charity; control cell; N not given
family: the first ingredient of what you are asked to do
why: The sprinkles are the beginning of a cake, so the hand has already started [mine]. Nothing frightening is shown for a frightening illness [mine].
for_client: A school for adults who want to garden: envelope with nine bean seeds and 'Plant them tonight. Come on Saturday and we will show you what they need next.' Film: seeds tumble on a dark table, one is pushed into earth.
source: Royal Mail MarketReach case study on getmemedia.com, 26 March 2012
doubt: Better chosen names went with the better pack; income is a projection.
depends_on: The thing sent is the first step of the act.

opening: [The car's own start button, in a box: press it and the dealer calls to bring you a test drive]
picture: A fine small box with a single real start-stop button in the middle, personal to the reader; one press sends the request.
seller: Land Rover — Range Rover Evoque, UK
beat: usual car mailings with a form or a link
result: 44% response, over 2,000 test drive requests
measured_by: The agency creative's case; DMA Awards 2019 Gold (Automotive, Best Use of Mail); over 2,000 requests
family: one real button, one press
why: A button begs to be pressed [mine]. The whole effort of booking has been done in advance by the seller [mine].
for_client: A heating engineer leaves a red push-button on the boiler: 'Press. I come.' Film: thumb on the button, cut to his van's lights turning on in the street.
source: Jeremy Tracy, portfolio case 'The Evoque Button' (DMA Awards 2019 Gold)
doubt: Told by its maker; about 4,600 recipients [mine: 2,000 / 0.44]; chosen by data; a costly piece; cars sold not given.
depends_on: A dear product, a short list, and somebody who really comes.

opening: [A table tennis bat through the letterbox, for a car 'like nothing you've ever seen on the road']
picture: A real table tennis bat comes through the letterbox to explain the car.
beat: not given
result: 2.8 per cent sales conversion and ROI of 70:1
measured_by: Campaign annual 2008; sales conversion and return
family: an odd thing in the post that is a joke about the product
why: Nobody throws away a bat before he knows why it came [mine]. The odd thing says 'odd car' without praise [mine].
for_client: A carpenter of crooked-wall wardrobes sends a ruler bent by three degrees: 'Your wall.' Film: the ruler rolls off a table; laid against a real wall it fits.
source: Campaign, 'Annual: Top 10 DM Campaigns', 12 December 2008
doubt: List and cost not given; current owners were probably on it [mine].
depends_on: A thing whose oddness means something.

opening: [A 'field guide to eggs': chocolate eggs drawn like wild birds' eggs in their nests]
picture: A mailer called a field guide, with beautiful illustrations of Easter eggs in their 'natural' habitats.
beat: not given
result: 15 per cent response, incremental sales of £2.2 million
measured_by: Campaign annual 2008; response and added sales
family: the goods shown as if they were found in nature
why: It is looked at like a book and kept, while a leaflet is thrown away [mine]. The reader discovers the joke himself, slowly [mine].
for_client: A paint shop's 'Field guide to whites': each white drawn as a moth with its name and where it lives ('north-facing kitchens'). Film: a hand turns the pages, one moth opens into a painted room; the price of a tester.
source: Campaign, 'Annual: Top 10 DM Campaigns', 12 December 2008
doubt: Sent to the shop's own customers before a festival; the festival itself need not be used.
depends_on: Craft good enough to pass for the real book.

opening: [An envelope with no address: only a hand-drawn map and directions to the reader's own door]
picture: Each envelope carries, instead of an address, the way to the man's office: head east from the airport until the boulevard, follow it north past the old market…
seller: what3words — address system, to heads of ten African postal services (OgilvyOne London)
beat: not given
result: eight of the ten replied (80%); one signed an annual contract, five countries adopted the system within a year
measured_by: International Post Corporation case; replies; N = 10
family: the envelope is the trouble itself
why: The reader, whose trade is delivering letters, feels the trouble in his own hand before he opens it [mine]. It arrived, so somebody took the pains it describes [mine].
for_client: A firm that labels warehouses sends managers a parcel marked 'third shelf, behind the blue boxes, next to the old printer, in your own store'. Film: the parcel really waits there, dusty; he opens it: a label and a number.
source: International Post Corporation, direct-marketing case studies: what3words
doubt: Ten people only; the five countries named are not among the ten addressed.
depends_on: Very few, very valuable readers; the trouble can be carried by the packet.

opening: [A cardboard teepee that unfolds in the hand, in a clear box: the invitation and the reply are folded in its floor]
picture: A clear plastic box through which one sees a tiny tent; taken out it stands, and the invitation pulls out of its bottom like an accordion.
seller: Camp Oochigeas, Toronto — summer camp for children with cancer
beat: not given
result: 600 sent, 400 bought tickets or gave; the event netted $88,000
measured_by: The Chronicle of Philanthropy on the award winners; N = 600
family: a little model of the place that is asked for
why: It is a toy of the very thing the money makes [mine]. A clear box cannot be mistaken for a bill [mine].
for_client: A house builder for small plots invites thirty families with a fold-up paper house whose roof lifts to show the open day's date. Film: two hands open it on a kitchen table, a child looks in.
source: The Chronicle of Philanthropy, 'Charities win honors in direct marketing contest'
doubt: The list was the camp's own circle; agency and printing were donated.
depends_on: A short list that already cares; a model made with love.

doubt: Print and radio advertising ran beside it; the court figures are the company's own, accepted by the court.
opening: "Can your radio do this? Only one radio gives you stereo sound this big, yet it's small enough to fit almost anywhere."
picture: 0 s: from black, the camera stands an inch from a small cream radio, looking down on its buttons and the name BOSE; 0.4-1.6 s: it pulls back and sinks to eye level in one smooth move until the whole radio sits small on an empty warm-grey wall; 2-3 s: a hand slides in from the right with a remote control, presses, the clock lights green and the hand goes; 4 s: the little radio rises and doubles itself upwards into a stack. No people, no set. (frames watched; words by speech model)
beat: the same first picture and the same first question were still on air three years later (a 1994 and a 1997 broadcast compared frame by frame)
result: $250 million (500,000 radios at $500) since 1993; $100 million a year; over $60 million of advertising paid for
measured_by: figures before the US Court of Appeals, Federal Circuit, Bose v. QSC, 2002; units since inception 500,000
family: a dare to what you own, answered by the thing alone
why: The question is asked of the radio the viewer already has, and the answer is a movement and not a claim. [mine] The empty wall leaves nothing else to look at. [mine]
for_client: Carpenter who makes folding tables: an empty room, a shelf 12 cm deep on the wall; a hand enters and pulls; "Can your table do this?" It opens for eight people in two seconds; "The wall table, made to your size — measured free this week."
source: Bose Corporation v. QSC Audio Products, 293 F.3d 1367 (Fed. Cir. 2002)
depends_on: The product must do one visible thing the common one cannot, in under three seconds, with nothing else in the frame.

doubt: Catalogues and shop advertising grew in the same year; in 2000 the show itself was a quarter of sales.
opening: "Limp vegetables, ruined fruit, freezer burn and moldy cheese — they're all now a thing of the past."

for_client: Bicycle repair shop: hand-held camera, two people in uniform knock at a garden shed at dawn: 'We've had reports of a bicycle left out since spring.' They carry the rusty bicycle out in a blanket; it ends on the shop's full service and its price
source: Marketing Week, Marmite's controversial ad sparks 14% sales uplift, 2014
doubt: The seller's own figure; more than 500 people complained, the regulator did not investigate. Sales before/after, no control group
depends_on: A format of programme the viewer knows by heart, played perfectly straight; something at home he has really forgotten

opening: "Shreddies are supposed to be square." (a factory supervisor's voice over the belt)
picture: 0-0.4 s black. 0.4-2.6 s: a white factory hall, a woman in hair net and white coat bends low over a conveyor, frowning at thousands of square wheat biscuits; the yellow Shreddies box stands behind her, the camera drifts slowly sideways. From 2.6 s: looking straight down the belt, only rows of square biscuits gliding towards us on white, for seconds, until one lies on its corner
seller: Post Shreddies (Canada) - 'Diamond Shreddies', film Factory Floor
beat: the same weeks of the previous year
result: +18% baseline sales within the first month of the national launch
measured_by: Canadian Marketing Association award report (Ogilvy); baseline sales against the previous year; N not given
family: an accident at the factory
why: A rule is stated flatly and the eye begins to hunt for the one that breaks it. The 'new' product is the old one turned by 45 degrees, so the viewer gets the joke himself and tells it [mine]
for_client: Furniture maker: a foreman at the line: 'A stool is supposed to have three legs.' A long row of identical stools passes, one lies upside down. 'New: the hat stand.' Ends on the stool, the price and the shop
source: Media in Canada, CMA awards report, 2008
doubt: TV, print, outdoor, web together; a humorous relaunch of an unchanged cereal, said openly as a joke
depends_on: The product must be so well known that the smallest change is visible at once, and the joke must be open, never a false claim

opening: On screen: "[Never Gonna Give You Up intro plays.]" then the singer sings it wrong: "and I'm gonna run around with dessert spoons"
picture: 0-2 s: from above, a man's two hands with a wedding ring put a cassette into an old recorder and press the key. 2-3 s: dark, his hand beats the rhythm on his knee. 3.2-4 s: Rick Astley and a producer with a guitar at a studio desk, smiling, warm lamp light; the subtitle names the song everyone knows. At 9 s the known line comes out wrong
beat: a target of 5% more bookings
result: hearing-test bookings +66% year on year in launch week against a target of 5%
measured_by: Specsavers, reported by Contagious (Cannes Lions PR Grand Prix 2024); N not given
family: the song you know, sung wrong
why: Everybody can check at once whether his ears deceive him, so the ad itself is a hearing test. The famous song makes him wait for the next wrong word [mine]
for_client: Optician: a well-known nursery rhyme's lines hang on a wall as posters; one letter is blurred in each and the mother reads them wrong aloud to her child; ends on the free sight check and the booking line
source: Contagious, Cannes Lions 2024 PR winners
doubt: The song was first let out on radio, in shops and online without a name; the film watched is the campaign's own film. The seller's figures
depends_on: A song the whole town knows, the right to change it, and a fault the changed words themselves prove

opening: (no speech) title card "Felix - SMOOTH OPERATOR", then a drawn cat's eyes rise above the table edge beside the tin
picture: 0-1.4 s: black card, gold hand-written 'felix', under it SMOOTH OPERATOR. 1.6 s: a black-and-white pencil drawing on pure white: two human hands turn a tin opener on the Felix tin; behind the table a black-and-white cat rises from chin to chest, stares, licks its lips. 3-4 s: its eyes follow the hand, then it leans and sniffs the lid. Only the cat moves; one line at the end: 'Cats like Felix like Felix'
beat: brand leader with far larger budgets
result: volume share 6.7% to 25.4% in seven years; GBP 17m of advertising led to GBP 108m of direct extra sales
measured_by: sales modelling by the agency, IPA Effectiveness paper reported by Marketing Week
family: a drawn cat that behaves like yours
why: It is the cheapest possible film, pencil on white, so the cat's behaviour is all there is to see, and every owner recognises it. The same character opened every film, so the brand was known in the first frame [mine]
for_client: Baker: a pencil drawing on white, a small boy's eyes rise above the counter edge while a hand lifts a warm roll from the basket; ends on the line of rolls and the hour they come out of the oven
source: Marketing Week, Felix catfood, 1990s
doubt: The figure is the campaign's, not this one film's; the 1994 film is one of the series, all opening with the same drawn cat
depends_on: An owner who sees his own animal in the drawing, and the same figure kept for years

also.source: Closer to Brands, Insight without an insight, 2017
also.result: market share 6.5% -> 42% in six years, number one in place of Whiskas

opening: "We asked real people if they'd help us with an experiment for Febreze Fabric Refresher. They agreed."
picture: 0-0.8 s: a busy New York pavement, a man in a light-blue shirt with papers stops passers-by, seen from a hidden camera; 'febreze experiment' stands at the bottom. 0.8-1.6 s: a woman in sunglasses nods. 1.6-3.4 s: hard cut to a filthy dark shed, two workers lay a wet dog on a stained couch and pull torn covers over it. 3.6 s: the blue spray bottle close up, a hand presses it over the couch
seller: Febreze Fabric Refresher (P&G) - 'Breathe Happy', film Couch
beat: sales before the campaign
result: +18.2% sales within 10 weeks of the campaign
measured_by: reported by Forbes, 2012 (the figure is linked there to its source); N not given
family: blindfolded strangers in the dirtiest room
why: The viewer is let into the trick and waits for the faces when the blindfold comes off. The dirtier the room, the stronger the proof, so the ugliness itself holds the eye [mine]
for_client: Carpet cleaner: ten neighbours are asked at the market, blindfolded, to lie down on a carpet and say where they are ('a hotel?'); the mask comes off: it is the garage floor of the mechanic next door, half cleaned. Ends on the price per square metre
source: Forbes, New Febreze advertising stands out in a crowded market, 2012
doubt: Second-hand figure in a columnist's text; the couch film is one of the campaign's experiments (hotel, car)
depends_on: The test must be real and the people unpaid strangers; the product's effect must be felt in the moment

opening: "Time to make the donuts." (a sleepy baker, going out of the door)
picture: 0-0.4 s black. 0.4-2.4 s: a dim hallway before dawn, a short man with a black moustache in baker's whites and paper hat shuffles to the door and opens it, purple night light outside; he says the line like a sigh. 2.6-4 s: he goes out; at once he comes in again by the same door, tired, and meets himself
beat: none given: kept on air for 15 years
result: the same baker ran for 15 years in an estimated 100 commercials
measured_by: the advertiser's own spending: 1982-1997, about 100 films
family: the man who must get up for you
why: One tired man says one line and the whole promise (fresh, twice a day) is understood without a claim. The door that opens twice makes the second watch as good as the first [mine]
for_client: Fruit market: 4 a.m., an old grocer in a wool cap pulls on his boots: 'Off to choose the tomatoes.' The door shuts; it opens; 'I chose the tomatoes.' Ends on the stall and today's price per kilo
source: Mental Floss, 13 things about Dunkin' Donuts' 'Time to make the donuts' guy
doubt: No sales figure; the proof is 15 years of paying for it. The film watched is an early one of the series (copy from a re-upload, year not printed)
depends_on: A true hardship behind the product, and an actor whose face carries it without words

opening: "Leftover chicken, scallions, cheese... What am I going to make with this?" - "Meow?"
picture: 0 s: we are inside a fridge, its door opens towards us, shelves with a wilted spring onion, a lump of cheese and a chicken dish. 0.4-2.2 s: a woman in a white knitted jumper leans in and searches, puzzled, face framed by the shelves. 2.4-3.4 s: cut to a fluffy grey cat on a red stool in a warm kitchen, staring. 3.6-4 s: she sets the things on the board, the cat's back in the foreground; the cat says the brand's name as a meow
beat: the brand's decline before
result: +12.7% dollar sales, +9% volume, +3% household penetration
measured_by: WARC case summary of the Hellmann's campaign; N not given
family: the fridge looks at you
why: Everyone has stood before that fridge with that question, and the camera stands where nobody can stand. The answer comes from the one who cannot speak, so the name is heard twice as a joke [mine]
for_client: Greengrocer: the camera lies in the vegetable drawer; a father bends in: 'Half a cabbage, one carrot... what is this?' The small son answers with one word, the shop's soup box; ends on the box and its price
source: WARC, Hellmann's: Mayo Cat, 2025
doubt: Figures are the campaign's (shop, social and the film together); a famous actress plays; an oath is half spoken at 10 s
depends_on: A household trouble recognised in one second, and the product as the plain answer to it

opening: (no English speech; a mother at the curtain at dawn) subtitle: "Hi Sweetie."
picture: After the studio slate: 0-0.8 s: a dark wet street before dawn, a cyclist with a lamp comes towards us past a gate tower. 0.8-2.2 s: a small blue room, a woman in silhouette draws a curtain from the window. 2.4-4 s: a small girl asleep on her arm under a flowered cover; the mother's hand comes in and strokes her shoulder awake. Piano, no product; other countries' mothers follow
seller: Procter & Gamble - 'Best Job', Thank You Mom, London Olympics
result: USD 500 million of added sales during the London Olympics
measured_by: P&G executives' own estimate, USA Today 2014
family: a mother wakes a child
why: The smallest daily act is shown before dawn in four countries, so the viewer remembers his own mother before he knows who speaks. The medal at the end is the mother's reward, and the seller only thanks her [mine]
for_client: Shoe shop before the school year: dark kitchen, a father ties a small boy's laces, the boy half asleep; the same hands, years later, untie them at a running track. Ends: 'Thank you, fathers' and the school-shoe price
source: USA Today, P&G rolls out Olympics thank-you ad, 2014
doubt: The company's own estimate for the whole Olympic programme in many countries; the film was its chief piece. Athletes in sports dress appear later
depends_on: A true debt of thanks shared by all viewers, and a seller modest enough to stay out until the end

opening: "Rei dos memes, patrimônio cultural brasileiro..." ("King of memes, cultural heritage of Brazil...")
picture: 0-2 s: from behind, a caramel-brown street dog sits on a wall over a wide Brazilian town under a blue sky, its ear lifting. 2-3 s: it turns its head slowly and looks to the side, noble, like a lion. 3.2 s: the sky becomes a flat blue-and-yellow painted board with a sun behind the dog's head; hand-painted letters slide in from both sides: REI DOS MEMES
beat: sales before the launch
result: +23.3% sales
measured_by: reported by Valor International on the WARC Effective ranking 2026; N not given
family: the country's stray as a king
why: A dog everybody has fed and nobody has adopted is filmed like a monarch, so the viewer smiles with pride before the hard fact comes (90% less chance of a home). It belongs to the whole people, so the brand speaks for them [mine]
for_client: Tea house: the chipped little tea glass of every workshop turns slowly on a plinth: 'King of the noon break, witness of every bargain...' then: 'and never once served hot enough.' Ends on the thermos it sells
source: Valor International, AlmapBBDO named world's most effective creative agency, 2026
doubt: The period behind the figure is not printed; a whole campaign (DNA study, registry, adoption) stood behind the film
depends_on: Something the whole country already loves and laughs about, and a true need behind it

opening: Video title: "NSFW. A hunter shoots a bear!" - "There's a bear behind you!" - "What?"
picture: Seen as a page of the video site: 0-1.2 s: a small yellow tent with a pink cloth in a forest clearing, hand-held. 1.2-2 s: the camera swings right, a bearded hunter squats by a fire, brushing his teeth. 2-4 s: he looks round at the shouting cameraman; the bear is behind the tent. At 30 s the film stops: shoot or not? He reaches out of the picture for the correction tape in the advert beside it and wipes the word 'shoots' from the title
beat: sales before
result: sales in Europe +30% from September to October 2010
measured_by: D&AD archive (Buzzman, Bic): 46 million views, sales figure from the seller; N not given
family: the film waits for your word
why: A danger is already running when the film begins, and it stops exactly where a choice is needed. The product does its real work, erasing a word, on the page around the film [mine]
for_client: Paint shop: 'A painter drops the bucket!' A can tips on a ladder over a white carpet; the film stops; the viewer writes what should happen instead and the shop's colour rolls over the old title. Ends on the tester pot's price
source: D&AD archive, A Hunter Shoots a Bear, 2011
doubt: Back-to-school weeks, no control group printed. The men swear in the first seconds: keep the shape, not the words
depends_on: A page whose own frame can be played with, and an ending for every answer a viewer may give

opening: "Warsaw. Winter, '96. Minus seventeen, and not a chargrilled chop in sight."
picture: 0-7 s: one slow push towards a huge grey block of flats in driving snow, bluish, almost no colour, wide cinema bars; a woman's dry newsreader voice begins at 3 s. 7-10 s: an old television picture close up, then in the dark a lock clicks; only then the spy-film command room and 'Commence Operation Boomerang'
seller: Meat & Livestock Australia - Australia Day lamb, 'Operation Boomerang'
beat: the weekly average
result: lamb sales +36.9% across the two campaign weeks (34.4% and 39.5%), by far the most successful on record
measured_by: Meat & Livestock Australia, weekly sales against the weekly average; N not given
family: a thriller about lunch
why: It opens as a cold spy film and the last word of the sentence is a lamb chop, so seriousness and joke arrive in one breath. The trouble is a homesick man's, and the dish is what he misses [mine]
for_client: Village dairy: 'Frankfurt. February. Minus nine, and not one spoon of real yoghurt.' Snow, a lonely tram stop; a small insulated parcel is carried through the night like a diplomatic case. Ends on the delivery box
source: MLA news, 2016 Australia Day lamb campaign most successful on record
doubt: A holiday when lamb always sells more; a joke in the middle (fire in a vegan's flat) drew many complaints, the watchdog dismissed them
depends_on: A film kind everybody recognises in two seconds, and a small homely thing to end it on

opening: "Every cigarette is doing you damage. This is part of an aorta, the main artery from the heart."
picture: 0-1 s: a sickly green kitchen at night, a man in an orange shirt stands at the stove, a table with papers in front. 1.2-1.8 s: extreme close-up, a finger turns the gas knob. 2-3 s: he bends to the flame with a cigarette. 3.2-4 s: the burning tip from the front fills the screen like a furnace, crackling. Then the camera follows the smoke down the throat, and gloved hands squeeze white fat out of an artery
seller: Australian National Tobacco Campaign - film Artery
beat: smoking before the campaign
result: 190,000 fewer smokers after the first phase
measured_by: government evaluation studies, cited by Cancer Council's Tobacco in Australia 14.4
family: inside the body, in real matter
why: The smoker's own small ritual is filmed so close that he feels it in his own throat, and then the camera goes where he never looks. It shows a fact, with no plea [mine]
for_client: Dentist: a hand lifts a sweet to the mouth, the crackle of the paper huge; the camera follows it along the gum to the one spot the brush does not reach. 'Every sweet leaves this.' Ends on the cleaning appointment
source: Tobacco in Australia, chapter 14.4
doubt: The figure is the campaign's first phase (Artery was its first film among three); a public cause, not a sale. A smoker is shown smoking, as the thing warned of
depends_on: A harm that is true and can be shown in real matter, and a viewer who does the act daily

opening: (song) "Here they come, yo..." - two hooded figures in a hallway pull back their hoods: they are hamsters
picture: 0-0.4 s black. 0.4-1.4 s: from behind, two figures in red and grey hoods stand at a bright doorway in a dark wallpapered hall. 1.6-3 s: in front, the red one pushes the hood back, a huge hamster face with round eyes appears, 'Hamstar' on the chest, a chain round the neck. 3-3.8 s: the two look at each other. 4 s: the door bursts into light; then street after street: hamsters in their car beside toasters and cardboard boxes on wheels
beat: the same months a year earlier
result: year-to-date sales +50.8%, best-ever monthly sales, second Kia to pass 10,000 in a month
measured_by: Kia Motors America sales report, Effie Gold 2011
family: hidden faces, then animals
why: Two dangerous-looking figures turn out to be the gentlest animal, so the fear becomes a laugh in three seconds. Then every rival is a household box on wheels: the choice is made by the eye [mine]
for_client: Baby-buggy shop: two hooded figures at a lift door turn round: they are lambs; they roll out with the buggy past people pushing shopping carts and wheelbarrows: 'this, or that'. Ends on the buggy and its price
source: Kia press release, hamsters win Gold Effie, 2011
doubt: Kia credits this film and the earlier hamster film together; the whole car market was recovering. Rap song
depends_on: A figure nobody expects in that place, and rivals that really look alike

opening: (no speech, music) a woman in red and yellow walks through a huge pale office
picture: 0-1 s: a wide, pale, over-lit open office; blurred arms and coffee cups swing past the lens; a woman in a yellow jumper and red skirt (the brand's colours) walks away from us down the middle. 1-2 s: she stands still, everybody works. 2-3 s: side view, she carries a pile of files past the desks, the camera gliding with her. 3-4 s: she passes two colleagues and the frame rests on them; on a yellow note she will draw two arches and raise her eyebrows
result: GBP 43.7m of incremental revenue
measured_by: McDonald's UK / Leo Burnett, Marketing Society award paper 2024 (econometrics)
family: no food, no logo, one secret sign
why: Nothing is being sold for a whole minute, so the viewer looks for the reason everyone rises; one lifted eyebrow explains it. He can copy the sign at once, and the country did [mine]
for_client: Kebab house near a bank: a quiet counter hall, a clerk taps twice on his watch; the next one taps; a line of people walks out smiling; no word. Ends on the door of the house and the lunch menu's price
source: Marketing Society paper, The Bravery Behind the Brows, 2024
doubt: The film was the launch of a year's campaign; the figure is the campaign's. Office women in fitted dresses
depends_on: A seller so well known that the sign alone names him

opening: On screen: "Liverpool Street Station / 11:00 am / 15th January 2009"
picture: 0.3-3.2 s: plain white type on black, three short lines: place, hour, date; station noise under it. From 3.4 s: a high, fixed, hidden-camera view of the station hall, hundreds of people crossing, nothing happening yet; at 10 s music comes from the loudspeakers and one man starts to dance
result: GBP 15 million incremental sales; payback GBP 1.46 for every GBP 1
measured_by: IPA Effectiveness Awards 2010 Silver (agency econometrics), PRWeek
family: place, hour, date - then nothing
why: Like a police record: a place, an hour and a date say that something happened here. The empty seconds after it make every passer-by a suspect [mine]
for_client: Tile maker: white on black 'Central station, platform 3 / 06:40 / Monday'; a hidden camera sees commuters stop one after another and look down: the floor has become a carpet of tiles overnight. Ends on the maker's name
source: PRWeek, IPA Effectiveness Awards 2010 Silver: T-Mobile
doubt: Several films and activities together; a crowd dances, men and women: use only the first ten seconds' shape
depends_on: A real event with real passers-by, filmed once; a stunt big enough to pay for the waiting

opening: On screen: "Outside a major tobacco company." - then, through a megaphone: "We're gonna leave this here for you so you can see what 1200 people actually look like."
picture: 0.4-1.6 s: from a roof, grey-blue winter street between towers, a white delivery van drives up; the small line of type gives the place. 2-2.4 s: its doors open, young people jump out. 2.8-3.2 s: from above again, figures run across the crossing. 3.4-4 s: gloved hands pull long white sacks out of the van: body bags, and they go on and on until the pavement is full
seller: American Legacy Foundation - truth, film Body Bags
beat: the trend without the campaign
result: youth smoking 25.3% to 18.0% (1999-2002), about 22% of the fall due to the campaign: roughly 300,000 fewer young smokers
measured_by: Farrelly et al., American Journal of Public Health 2005, Monitoring the Future surveys 1997-2002 with dose-response model
family: a number laid out on the street
why: It looks like news footage of something forbidden going on, so one watches before knowing the side. The number nobody can picture is laid out, sack by sack, until it is seen [mine]
for_client: Water-filter seller: 'Outside the town hall.' A lorry opens and volunteers stand 1,460 empty plastic bottles on the steps: 'One family, one year.' Ends on one glass jug and its price
source: Farrelly et al., AJPH 2005 (PMC1449196)
doubt: The figure is the national campaign's, of which this was the best-known film; a cause, not a sale
depends_on: A true count that fits on a street, and an address where it belongs

opening: On screen over old home films: "When you were a baby your mother gave you hugs."
picture: 0-1.8 s: a 1970s home film, warm grain: a young mother on a garden chair laughs with a newborn in a white blanket and a toddler at her knee. 2-2.6 s: another mother in a green jumper, dark curls, lifts her eyes to the camera. 2.8-4 s: over her and the sleeping baby a hand-written line fades in, then bold: 'your mother gave you hugs.' Then, line by line, what those hugs did to the child's heart, growth and brain, and today's grandmothers holding today's mothers
seller: Huggies (Kimberly-Clark Canada) - 'No Baby Unhugged', launch film Power of Hugs
beat: category growing 1% a year; own share falling 36.6% to 34.9% before
result: newborn diaper dollar volume +19.2%, nearly double the 10% goal
measured_by: AC Nielsen MarketTrack, CASSIES Grand Prix 2017 case
family: your own beginning, in old film
why: It speaks to the mother as the child she was, in the pictures of her own years, so she is moved before she is sold to. The tenderness is then given a doctor's reason [mine]
for_client: Photo studio: shaky films of fathers carrying small children on their shoulders, 1980s colours: 'When you were small, somebody carried you.' The same men, old, now lifted into a car. Ends on the family portrait day and its price
source: CASSIES, Huggies - No Baby Unhugged, 2017
doubt: The launch film and three documentary films, a hospital hugging programme and online ads worked together; mothers holding bare newborns later in the film
depends_on: Old pictures the viewer recognises as his own time, and a proven reason behind the feeling

opening: Tweet in reply to a rival's "all the love for the original": "... y'all good?"
beat: the week before; rivals in the same fight
result: visits +54% after the exchange (45 million phones); store sales +34% Aug 2019-Feb 2020; sandwich sold out
measured_by: Bhave, Kamatham, Bruce (phone-location data, 45 million users), Chicago Booth Review; Effie Grand 2021: +13% same-store sales, USD 1bn
family: two words to the rival
why: It answers a boast with a calm, almost kind question, so the crowd says the rest. The fight made everyone taste both, and the smaller house gained most [mine]
for_client: Corner bakery: the supermarket posts 'Bread. Flour. Water. Since 1990.' The baker answers under it with a photo of his queue at seven in the morning and two words: 'all well?'
source: Chicago Booth Review, Who won the Twitter fight
doubt: A new and very good product stood behind it; the tweet alone could not be separated from the whole exchange
depends_on: A bigger rival who speaks first, a real product that can be compared the same day, and a light hand

opening: "introducing the #WhopperDetour. order a Whopper for a penny only “at” McDonald’s with the BK app. yes, you read that right."
beat: its earlier digital promotions (40 times bigger than its record)
result: over 1.5 million app downloads in nine days; app sales value tripled during the promotion and doubled since; USD 15m incremental, ROI 37:1
measured_by: Effie Grand 2020 and One Show entry (FCB New York); app data
family: go to the rival, get it for a penny
why: The price is absurd and the place is forbidden, so the sentence has to be read twice. The rival's 14,000 houses become the seller's signs [mine]
for_client: Small hardware shop: 'A hammer for one lira, only if you order it on our page while standing in the car park of the big store. Yes, you read that right.' The map then leads him two streets on
source: One Show archive, The Whopper Detour, 2019
doubt: A nearly free burger for nine days; the words are the launch tweet as printed in the press (search extract of the news page)
depends_on: A rival with many houses, a way to check where the buyer stands, and a true one-penny price

opening: "This room will make you feel like you're living in a painting. It's decorated in a Post-Impressionist style, reminiscent of Southern France and times gone by." (an Airbnb listing signed Vincent, USD 10 a night)
picture: The listing's first photograph: a real bedroom that is Van Gogh's painting: crooked blue-green walls, yellow wooden bed with red cover, two rush chairs, brush strokes painted on floor and furniture, seen from the painter's angle
seller: Art Institute of Chicago - Van Gogh's Bedrooms exhibition
beat: projected attendance
result: 133,000 incremental visitors and USD 2 million incremental revenue on USD 500,000
measured_by: Cannes Creative Effectiveness Grand Prix 2017, reported by Adweek (Leo Burnett Chicago)
family: the exhibit as a room to let
why: An impossible thing stands in a place for ordinary things, in the ordinary form: price, beds, host. One wants to check whether it is real, and it is [mine]
for_client: Carpet dealer: on the house-letting site, 'One night on a flying carpet, 10 euros': a small attic room with a carpet hung on four wires like a swing; host 'Aladdin' gives a voucher for the shop. Ends on the season's carpets
source: Adweek, Van Gogh Bnb takes the Creative Effectiveness Grand Prix, 2017
doubt: The exhibition itself was great news; listing words from the press (Chicagoist, Business Insider extracts). Posters and a film also ran
depends_on: A thing that can really be built once and really be rented, and a platform where nobody expects it

opening: "The Best Job in the World. Position Vacant: Island Caretaker. Location: Islands of the Great Barrier Reef, Queensland, Australia. Salary: AUD$150,000 six-month contract. Responsibilities: Clean the pool, Feed the fish, Collect the mail, Explore and report back ... Anyone can apply."
picture: A small black-bordered classified box on a newspaper's jobs page: heavy capitals THE BEST JOB IN THE WORLD., four short facts under it, at the foot ANYONE CAN APPLY and the address; filmed in the case: the camera moves over the grey page among other small ads
seller: Tourism Queensland - Islands of the Great Barrier Reef
result: 34,684 one-minute video applications; over 4 million unique visitors in 28 days
measured_by: One Show entry (SapientNitro / CumminsNitro), site and application counts
family: a holiday written as a vacancy
why: The longed-for place is not praised, it is offered as work with a salary and dull duties, in the driest form a newspaper has. Anyone can apply turns a reader into a candidate [mine]
for_client: Beekeeper's village shop: 'Vacant: honey taster. Place: the flowering hill above the village, June. Pay: a kilo a day. Duties: eat bread, say which jar is best. Anyone can apply.' Ends on the June tasting weekend
source: One Show archive, The Best Job in the World, 2009
doubt: Counts applications and visits, not bookings; the advert text is from a page that prints it and from the case film
depends_on: A real job, really paid, in a place people dream of

also.source: AEF: The Best Job in the World, digital marketing case study
also.result: 34,684 one-minute video applications from 197 countries (target 10,000), reach over 3 billion through media; A$1 million budget

opening: "Does she... or doesn't she? Hair color so natural only her hairdresser knows for sure!"
picture: A wholesome, freshly dressed young mother beside her child, hair of the same colour, in a colour photograph; no salon, no bottle in the hand (as described by the agency's histories; the scan was not seen)
seller: Clairol - Miss Clairol hair colour bath (Foote, Cone & Belding)
result: sales +413% in six years
measured_by: Inc. magazine letter, 1986 (agency's figure); Wikipedia: USD 25m to 200m a year of hair colour sales
family: a question about somebody else
why: It asks a question whose answer nobody can see, which is exactly the benefit. The mother and the child take the doubt out of the question [mine]
for_client: Invisible-mending tailor: a coat on a hanger, nothing else: 'Was it torn... or wasn't it? Only our tailor knows.' Ends on the price of a mend

depends_on: A working thing on camera; a longing already in the air.

opening: (music) | screen: people send me photos of their dogs as puppies & adults. this is what I do with them:

family: people send me X, this is what I do:
why: The colon is a door left open [mine]. The colourless face holds back all colour for the pictures that follow [mine].
for_client: Frame and photo shop: the owner, grey apron, says nothing. Screen: 'People bring me the only photo they have of their grandfather. This is what I do with it:' Beat: torn print, then whole; faded, then clear. Ends: bring one, ready in three days, price.
source: CNBC Make It — This 35-year-old spends $55 a month photoshopping dogs, 2022
doubt: the half-year, not the film alone
depends_on: The result must move in one picture; orders must be simple.

opening: (song) | screen: I made the Locket widget for my girlfriend / When either of us sends a photo, it appears on the other's Home Screen

family: I made this for one person
why: Made for one person is the opposite of an advert for all [mine]. The whole use is shown in one press of the thumb [mine].

opening: So I'm getting ready for work and I wanted to share something with you guys. Do you see all these bags under my eyes? I'm 54.
picture: 0-3.5 s: an older woman on a porch, hair in a grey towel turban, no make-up, bags under the eyes in plain daylight, earrings, speaks slowly to the phone at arm's length; nothing moves but the face. (Then she puts a little on one bag and waits; it flattens as we watch.)
seller: Peter Thomas Roth — Instant FIRMx Eye (customer Trinidad Sandoval's film)
result: six months' normal sales in under a week, sold out at every retailer; film 44.1m views (account had about 70 followers)
measured_by: founder Peter Thomas Roth, Glossy and Beauty Independent, August 2021
family: customer shows the flaw first, then lets it run in real time
why: The flaw, the age and the towel come before any praise [mine]. One take, three minutes, could have failed on camera [mine].
for_client: Silver polisher: a customer at her kitchen table, morning robe closed to the neck: 'I want to show you something. See this teapot? It is my mother's, it is black.' One wipe on one half, then she waits and turns it. Ends: the tin, the shop in the arcade.
source: Glossy — Meet TikTok's newest star Trinidad Sandoval, 2021
doubt: bare shoulders; effect is temporary, as the product says
depends_on: The change must be real, quick and visible in one take; unpaid customer.

opening: (music) | screen: want clear skin?
picture: 0-1 s: a young woman in a grey zip jumper holds a small red bottle beside her cheek. 1-2 s: the label fills the frame. 2-2.5 s: by a window a dropper lifts blood-red liquid from the bottle. 2.5-3.5 s: the red drop runs down her cheek. Four shots in three seconds.

why: Three words ask, the red answers with a shock: is that blood [mine]. The second film of the same hour showed the old skin, so the promise had a face [mine].
for_client: Parquet oiler: Screen: 'want your floor back?' Shots on the beat: tin beside a grey board, the label, honey-dark oil dripping from the brush, the first stroke lighting one plank. Ends: one litre, one room, at the hardware counter.
source: Vogue Business — Affordable beauty brands are finding fame on TikTok, 2020

opening: So I just got these Peace Out pore strips in the mail… | (left half: a known skin adviser waves and watches) caption: SO satisfying! I love these things
picture: 0-1 s: split screen: left, a young man in a dark flowered shirt waves and grins; right, a young woman lifts a white box with a hand sign to the lens. 1-3.5 s: the box fills her half; he pulls a doubtful mouth, then suddenly holds up the same box. (Later she peels the strip off and he opens his mouth.)

why: We read the judge's face for the verdict while the trial runs beside him [mine]. He says nothing in the first seconds, only his mouth tells [mine].

seller: Glow Recipe — Watermelon toner and Dew Drops (Mikayla Nogueira's film on Glamzilla's)

family: I saw this, I want that, I test it
why: The wish is spoken by one person and tested by another, so both halves are trusted [mine]. 'That all of you have been asking about' shows the demand first [mine].
for_client: Carpenter's oil: opens with another maker's clip, a table top glowing in a window. Cut: our joiner in his dusty shop: 'I want that.' He wipes one half of a grey board and does not speak until it dries. Ends: the tin, his shop, Saturday.

opening: Can Vaseline revive tired old leather? We're Vaseline's dedicated department working around the clock to verify hacks… | (nothing written at first)
picture: 0-2 s: blue-steel laboratory, a tired brown leather bag lies on a steel table like a patient, electrodes taped to it, a green heart monitor above it going flat. 2-3 s: a white ghost of the bag rises out of it. 3 s: alarm voice, 'This bag needs urgent attention', gloved hands.

for_client: Ironmonger's bench: 'Does vinegar really free a rusty lock?' The padlock lies on a white cloth, stethoscope on it, the apprentice in a lab coat. Clock on. It opens, or it does not, and the shop stamps the board either way. Ends: the thing that did work, on the hook by the till.

opening: Warro! Wait a minute, don't scroll down! Take a seat, I've got something important to tell you. | screen: Warro! / Wait a minute, / doe scroll down!
picture: 0-1 s: an old man in flat cap and waistcoat in a rocking chair by a coal fire in a dark Victorian room turns his head to us. 1-3.5 s: he leans in and stretches a flat palm at the lens to stop the thumb, dialect captions above him.
seller: Black Country Living Museum — Dudley, England ('1920s grandad')
result: account from nothing to 570,000 followers in six months; bookings interest of 18-24-year-olds on the site up 15 per cent; film 2.5m views
measured_by: the museum, Association of Independent Museums and the Association for Cultural Enterprises, 2021
family: a man from another time stops your thumb
why: A hand held up against a thumb is a gesture nobody passes by [mine]. 'Don't scroll' in a 1920s mouth is the joke and the welcome in one [mine].
for_client: Clock museum or antique dealer: an old man in a leather apron looks up from a watch, glass in his eye: 'You with the fast thumb. One minute. I have forty thousand of them here.' He opens the case, it chimes. Ends: open till five, the shop on Bell Lane.

doubt: the whole account grew; the museum was closed much of that time; the 2021 and 2022 visitor rises also follow the end of closures

opening: Hi. Tom Bodett here for Motel 6 with a comparison. You know, in some ways, a Motel 6 reminds me of one of those big, fancy hotels. They've got beds; we've got beds.
beat: six years of falling occupancy; the year before
result: 1987 occupancy +6 percentage points on 1986, nearly 3 more by 1989; revenue $256 million -> $297 million (+16%), then +14% and +25%
measured_by: Company figures printed in the Cornell Hotel and Restaurant Administration Quarterly case
family: plain man compares himself with the grand rival and loses on purpose
why: He admits everything the cheap room lacks in a friendly voice, so the price sounds like wisdom and not like poverty [mine]. The comparison lets the listener feel clever for not paying for avocado balm [mine].
for_client: Family dentist, radio or Reel: 'Hi, Hasan here from the little clinic on the corner, with a comparison. The big clinic has a chair; we've got a chair. They've got a waterfall in the lobby. We've got Tuesday at nine.' Ends: book Tuesday at nine.

also.result: revenue USD 256m to 297m, 1986 to 1987 (+16%), then +14% and +25%; followed by more than 100 spots over five years

opening: (voice, storyteller) "…And all across the land, the good folks of WestJet had a miracle planned." | screen: 'Twas a Night Before Christmas…

opening: "My friends. My sweet, sweet friends. I believe that finding the right apartment, through the right source and in the right way, can lead you… to the realized life."

opening: "When I grow up, I want to file all day." (a child, in all seriousness)

opening: "This man right here is my great-grandfather. He was the first cat herder in our family." (a cowboy, dead serious)

opening: "Okay, Eunice, travel plans. I need to be in New York on Monday, L.A. on Tuesday, New York on Wednesday, L.A. on Thursday, New York on Friday. Got it?" (at an impossible speed)

doubt: No sales figure for this one film; the campaign of five years was paid for and awarded; first words corrected by sense from a machine transcript
